justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 252.5 was anchored closely to the most recent observed price, with only a small expected move given typical daily volatility and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts. The one-week estimate of 253.5 incorporated a slight continuation of near-term momentum while acknowledging mean-reverting tendencies. The one-month estimate of 255.0 assumed a gradual drift consistent with longer-run trend expectations, though with diminishing confidence the further out the horizon extended. In all three cases, the estimates were not dramatic departures from the starting level, reflecting a view that the asset was near fair value with no strong directional conviction.

The width of the confidence intervals was primarily driven by historical volatility scaled to each time horizon in the standard square-root-of-time fashion. At one day, the interval of 247 to 258 is relatively tight, consistent with typical daily price fluctuations for an asset of this type. At one week, the interval widens to 243 to 264, reflecting the compounding of daily uncertainty over five trading sessions. By one month, the interval expands substantially to 235 to 275, capturing the much larger range of plausible outcomes over roughly twenty trading days. Additional uncertainty at longer horizons stemmed from macroeconomic conditions, earnings or policy announcements that could occur within the window, and general market sentiment shifts that are difficult to predict in advance.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sudden tightening of financial conditions, geopolitical escalation, or a sector-specific shock could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings release, dovish policy surprises, or a broad risk-on sentiment rally could push prices above the upper bounds. Liquidity events, flash crashes, or correlated forced selling across markets represent tail risks that my intervals do not fully capture since they are calibrated to normal distributional assumptions rather than fat-tailed scenarios. These possibilities, while assigned low probability, are real enough that realized outcomes falling outside my stated ranges would not be entirely surprising.
